screens.title: The Incident Lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: The incident lifecycle is the backbone of predictable operations. At its core there are five phases: detection, triage and assessment, response and mitigation, resolution, and post-mortem and learning. Detection means noticing an anomaly—an alarm, metric deviation, or user report. Triage and assessment is the rapid decision-making step: determine severity, scope, and potential impact. Response and mitigation are immediate actions to reduce impact, like restarting a service or scaling capacity. Resolution confirms full service restoration and documents closure criteria. Finally, post-mortem and learning capture root cause analysis and action items to prevent recurrence. A common misconception is to treat post-mortems as blame sessions; instead, they are fact-based learning exercises with clear action items. For example, if a web tier experiences sustained high C P U, detection might be a CloudWatch alarm. During triage you would check instance metrics and recent deployments. The response could include restarting the process or scaling out the Auto Scaling Group. After service is restored, the post-mortem describes the root cause and updates the runbook. Emphasize measurable closure criteria so everyone agrees when an incident is truly resolved. What measurable signal will you use to close the next incident?

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle summary
keyIdea.text: Adopt the five-phase lifecycle to make incidents predictable: Detect → Triage → Respond → Resolve → Learn.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.5 › Incident Lifecycle
Definition
A repeatable sequence of phases that turn detection into learning and improvements.
Detection
Monitoring alerts, user reports, or health checks that show an issue exists.
Triage & Assessment
Quickly determine severity, affected scope, and immediate risks to data or customers.
Response & Mitigation
Actions to reduce impact and restore partial or full service.
Resolution
Confirming service is restored and applying closure criteria before marking incident closed.
Example scenario
CloudWatch alarm fires for sustained high CPU on a production EC2 instance. Detection is the alarm. In triage, check metrics, instance health, and recent deployments to assess if it is application code or infrastructure. Response might restart the app service or scale the Auto Scaling Group. Resolution is when CPU stabilizes and user errors stop. Post-mortem documents root cause and updates the runbook to include additional monitoring thresholds or a new mitigation step.
Key Takeaway

A lifecycle makes response predictable and ensures incidents convert into team learning.

Common mistake
Skipping post-mortems or not defining closure criteria, which leaves work uncompleted.

screens.title: Severity Levels and Impact Assessment
screens.narratorSegment: Severity levels are the shorthand your team uses to decide response intensity. The chapter suggests four levels: Severity 1 critical, Severity 2 high, Severity 3 medium, and Severity 4 low. A Severity 1 might be a major service outage with widespread customer impact or data loss, requiring an immediate all-hands response. Severity 2 indicates major functionality is impaired but without data loss, needing urgent attention. Severity 3 covers limited impact with workarounds available and can be scheduled, while Severity 4 is cosmetic or non-urgent. To apply these consistently, use an impact assessment that considers affected user count, financial loss, data integrity, and compliance implications. Misconceptions occur when teams base severity only on loudness — a single high-value customer outage deserves higher severity even if user count is small. Use examples: a degraded payment A P I affecting checkout for 10% of users is higher impact than a cosmetic UI glitch for 90% of users. Document clear thresholds in your incident policy — for instance, number of affected users or error rate percentage — and practice assigning severities during drills. This makes escalation and resource allocation predictable and reduces debate during real incidents.

keyIdea.text: Define severity by customer impact, data risk, and financial/compliance implications rather than loudness alone.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.5 › Severity & Impact
Severity levels
Severity 1 (Critical)
Major outage, widespread customer impact, or data loss — immediate all-hands response.
Severity 2 (High)
Key functionality impaired, significant customer impact, urgent response required.
Severity 3 (Medium)
Limited impact with workaround; schedule remediation.
Severity 4 (Low)
Cosmetic or minor issues; non-urgent fixes.
Impact assessment criteria
  • Number of affected users or percentage of traffic impacted.
  • Financial cost or revenue impact per minute or hour.
  • Data integrity concerns: risk of loss or corruption.
  • Compliance and legal implications for the business.
Practical example
A payment API that fails for 10% of users may be Severity 2 because it affects revenue, whereas a visual layout bug for many users may be Severity 4.
Common mistake
Setting severity by vocality rather than measured impact; codify thresholds to avoid arguments during incidents.

screens.title: Runbooks: Structure and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Runbooks (or playbooks) turn incident knowledge into action. A good runbook includes the incident title and type, clear trigger conditions, a pre-assigned severity, initial triage steps, mitigation steps, troubleshooting, communication and escalation plans, resolution criteria, and post-mortem requirements. This structure ensures responders can act quickly and consistently. The trigger must be specific—naming the alarm and threshold prevents confusion. Initial triage is short and focused: validate the alarm, confirm affected resources, and collect metrics. Mitigation steps are ordered, with safe actions first. Troubleshooting includes deeper diagnostics and commands, while the communication plan lists who to notify and the frequency of updates. Escalation identifies who to call if the primary responder fails to resolve the issue. Keep runbooks living: update them after every incident and after drills. A common misconception is to overload runbooks with too many possible branches; instead, aim for a short, reliable path to reduce cognitive load during stress and reference deeper diagnostics as appendices. Practice the runbook in drills so responders can follow it reflexively. Runbooks: Structure and Best Practices means use concise, ordered steps with clear triggers, mitigation, comms, escalation, and resolution criteria. keep runbooks small and test them.. In practical terms, what each playbook should include and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 12 › Chapter 12.5 › Runbook Structure
Runbook template
Incident Title/Type
A concise name, e.g., "High CPU on Production EC2 Instance".
Trigger Conditions
Which alarms or symptoms start the runbook, with precise thresholds.
Initial Triage Steps
Quick checks to verify the incident and gather context, such as metric snapshots and recent deployments.
Mitigation & Troubleshooting
Ordered, tested actions to restore service and commands to gather diagnostics.
Communication & Escalation
List contact roles, channels, and update cadence. Define who to escalate to and when.
Resolution & Post-Mortem
Clear criteria to close the incident and a requirement to perform a post-mortem when thresholds are met.
Pro Tip
Keep the primary mitigation steps short and tested. Put longer diagnostics as appendices.

screens.title: Runbook Walkthrough: High CPU on Web Server
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a simplified runbook for "High C P U on Web Server." The trigger is a CloudWatch alarm named WebTier-HighCPU entering the ALARM state. The initial triage step is to verify the alarm by fetching CPUUtilization for the instance ID and confirming sustained high values. Then check top processes by SSHing into the instance and running top or a process list to identify C P U consumers. Review recent deployments in the CI/CD pipeline to see if a new release correlates with the spike. For mitigation, if the C P U is caused by an application process, restart that service. If it's infrastructure load, scale out the Auto Scaling Group or replace the instance. Communicate status to the incident channel after each major action. Confirm resolution when C P U returns to normal and user errors stop. A misconception is to restart immediately without collecting evidence; instead, gather quick diagnostics first so the post-mortem has context. Practice this runbook, and if you automate any steps, ensure they are reversible and tested in non-production. Below you will see the commands typically used for diagnosis and the mitigation actions as a readable code panel.

keyIdea.title: Runbook example
keyIdea.text: Verify alarm, gather metrics, identify process cause, then mitigate with restart or scaling; document and communicate every step.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.5 › Runbook Example
Runbook: High CPU on Web Server
Trigger: CloudWatch Alarm: WebTier-HighCPU in ALARM state. Severity: 2 (High).
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUUtilization --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx --start-time 2022-01-01T12:00:00Z --end-time 2022-01-01T12:05:00Z --period 300 --statistic Average

ssh -i key.pem ec2-user@<instance-ip>
# then run
top
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -n 10

aws codepipeline list-pipeline-executions --pipeline-name MyWebAppPipeline --max-items 5

# Mitigation examples
sudo systemctl restart my-web-app.service
aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name MyWebAppASG --desired-capacity 4
Explanation
  • Verify the alarm with metric statistics to avoid false positives.
  • Gather process lists to identify the root cause before restarting services.
  • Check CI/CD for recent deployments that may have introduced regressions.
  • Choose mitigation that matches cause: app restart vs. scaling.
Key Takeaway
Collect evidence before action and make mitigations reversible where possible.

screens.title: Automating Remediation with EventBridge + Systems Manager
screens.narratorSegment: Automation can accelerate recovery, but it must be designed and tested carefully. AWS Systems Manager Automation provides runbooks-as-code that perform operations such as restarting instances or scaling groups. Amazon EventBridge acts as the event router: CloudWatch alarms emit a change-of-state event, EventBridge matches it with a rule, and the rule can target an SSM Automation document for execution. A common pattern is to match CloudWatch Alarm State Change events where the alarm name equals your high C P U alarm, then configure the rule to start AWS-RestartEC2Instance or a custom document that scales an Auto Scaling Group. Important safety practices include limiting automation to narrowly scoped actions, using an execution role with least privilege, testing automation in a non-production environment, and designing idempotent steps. A key misconception is to automate wide-ranging destructive actions without reversibility; instead, automate small, reversible remediations first and require manual approval for high-risk changes. Logging automation executions and requiring an approval step for certain conditions preserves control while still enabling fast automated recovery where appropriate. Automating Remediation with EventBridge + Systems Manager means use eventbridge to route alarm events to ssm automation documents; prefer small, tested, reversible automations with least-privilege roles.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. keyIdea.text: Use EventBridge to route alarm events to SSM Automation documents; prefer small, tested, reversible automations with least-privilege roles.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.5 › Automation Architecture
Pattern
CloudWatch alarm → EventBridge rule → SSM Automation document. The Automation document runs with an IAM execution role to perform the remediation.
EventBridge rule
Match CloudWatch Alarm State Change events for the named alarm and route them to SSM.
SSM Automation
Runbooks-as-code such as AWS-RestartEC2Instance perform the action; custom documents can scale ASGs or run scripts.
Security
Use least-privilege roles for Automation execution and require approval steps for high-risk changes.
Event pattern example
{
  "source": ["aws.cloudwatch"],
  "detail-type": ["CloudWatch Alarm State Change"],
  "detail": {
    "alarmName": ["WebTier-HighCPU"],
    "state": { "value": ["ALARM"] }
  }
}
Safety note
Test automations in non-production and ensure execution roles have only the permissions needed for the action.

screens.title: Connecting a CloudWatch Alarm to Automation (Hands-on Flow)
screens.narratorSegment: This flow outlines the hands-on activity: create a CloudWatch alarm, choose an Automation document, create an EventBridge rule, and test safely. Step one, create a CloudWatch alarm for the EC2 instance's CPUUtilization metric. For testing, a low threshold can help validate the flow. Step two, identify or create an SSM Automation document—using AWS-RestartEC2Instance is a common choice because it encapsulates the restart steps. Ensure the Automation execution role has only the permissions required: ec2:RebootInstances and describe. Step three, create an EventBridge rule that matches the alarm state change and adds the SSM Automation document as the target. Pass the instance ID from the event into the Automation parameter so the document knows which instance to act on. Step four, test in a non-production instance by inducing C P U load and observing the alarm, EventBridge event, and Automation execution. Monitor the Automation execution log and the instance state transitions. Common mistakes include using overly broad IAM permissions, not passing instance identifiers from the event, and failing to validate that the Automation behaves as expected. Always test and review logs before enabling in production.

Step-by-step flow

Metric: EC2 → Per-Instance → CPUUtilization. Use a test-friendly threshold for validation.

screens.title: Playbook Components: Communication and Escalation
screens.narratorSegment: Communication is a core part of incident response. A runbook should include a communication plan that names who to notify, the channels to use, and what the message should contain at each update cadence. For high-severity incidents, notifications might include an incident channel, paging on-call leads, and notifying a service owner. Each update should state the current impact, actions taken, next steps, and an ETA if available. Escalation paths are explicit: identify primary and secondary responders and the conditions that trigger escalation, for example, no resolution in X minutes or rising error rates despite mitigation. Misconceptions include assuming responders will know whom to contact—explicit contact names or role placeholders remove ambiguity. Also note frequency: too many status messages can distract responders, too few leave stakeholders uninformed. Use short, templated messages in the runbook for each stage: initial acknowledgement, after triage, after mitigation, and on resolution. This practice keeps both technical and business stakeholders aligned and reduces noisy ad-hoc updates. screens.title: Post-Mortem and Learning
screens.narratorSegment: Post-mortems close the loop by extracting learning from incidents. A useful post-mortem documents the timeline, root cause analysis, contributing factors, and concrete action items with owners and due dates. Avoid blame language; the goal is system improvement. Include evidence collected during triage and response: metrics, logs, commands executed, and Automation execution details. Derive measurable actions: change a threshold, add a test, tighten IAM on an Automation role, or add observability for an uncovered gap. Mistakes to avoid are leaving action items without owners or not validating that fixes were implemented. Treat post-mortems as living artifacts—link them to runbook updates and schedule follow-up checks. For example, if automation restarted an instance but did not scale an ASG, an action item might be to modify the Automation document or add an additional step to scale out under sustained load. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: Common mistakes in incident automation and playbooks can make incidents worse rather than better. Outdated playbooks that don't reflect current architecture create confusion. Lack of clear ownership means nobody updates or executes the runbook reliably. With automation, the biggest risks come from overly broad permissions, untested scripts, or automations that make irreversible changes. A safety example: an Automation document that terminates instances without verifying Auto Scaling Group health can reduce capacity further. To avoid these issues, enforce least-privilege IAM roles for Automation, test documents in non-production, prefer reversible or non-destructive remedial steps, log every execution, and include an approval step for high-risk actions. Practicing runbooks in drills reveals gaps and trains responders. A useful contrast: manual mitigation is slower but safer for complex, novel incidents; automation is faster for well-understood, repeatable problems. Use both thoughtfully — automate the repeatable, keep human oversight for ambiguous situations, and keep your playbooks updated from every post-mortem. fullNarratorScript:
Incidents will happen even in well-run systems. In this lesson you will learn the structured lifecycle for incidents, how to assign consistent severity levels, and how to write practical incident response playbooks that your team can follow under pressure. We will then show how automation can safely speed recovery by connecting CloudWatch alarms to AWS Systems Manager Automation through EventBridge. You will see a concrete runbook for a "High C P U" event, learn what to automate and what to keep manual, and review common mistakes that make automation dangerous. By the end you will understand how to prioritize incidents, what belongs in a runbook, and how to test an automation workflow in a non-production environment. This matters because clear playbooks and controlled automation reduce time-to-recovery, avoid confusion during stress, and make post-incident learning actionable. Consider an outage where engineers scramble without guidance: the time cost and risk rise. A practiced runbook and tested automation turns that chaos into repeatable steps and measurable improvement. Reflect: which small automation could save your team ten minutes during the next incident?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define the incident lifecycle and name its phases, set consistent severity and impact criteria, author practical incident response playbooks, and wire CloudWatch alarms to Systems Manager Automation via EventBridge for safe remediation. Each objective focuses on a skill you can practice: identifying and triaging incidents quickly, deciding when an event is critical versus routine, writing step-by-step runbook actions and communications, and automating repeatable safe operations while avoiding automation hazards. For example, when you write a runbook for high C P U you will include clear trigger conditions, initial triage commands, mitigation steps, and who to notify — and you will test any automatic restart in a non-production environment. Practicing these objectives reduces confusion under stress, shortens recovery time, and embeds lessons into your team's operational playbooks. Think of this as learning both the cookbook and the safe way to run the tools.

These objectives are practical. Defining an incident lifecycle gives you a shared language so team members know when to escalate. Clear severity levels prevent lengthy debates about priorities and direct the right resources to high-impact events. Authoring runbooks codifies tribal knowledge into a step-by-step guide a junior responder can follow during a crisis. Finally, automating safe mitigations shortens the time between detection and recovery while freeing responders for diagnostics. An example: a CloudWatch alarm for sustained high C P U could either inform the team or trigger an automated Systems Manager Automation document that attempts a restart; the playbook decides the right course based on severity and testing. Note the important misconception to avoid: automation is not a substitute for an accurate runbook. Automation should implement discrete, well-tested actions defined in the runbook and guarded by least-privilege IAM and test procedures. Use drills to validate your runbooks and automations so they behave predictably when real incidents occur.

The incident lifecycle is the backbone of predictable operations. At its core there are five phases: detection, triage and assessment, response and mitigation, resolution, and post-mortem and learning. Detection means noticing an anomaly—an alarm, metric deviation, or user report. Triage and assessment is the rapid decision-making step: determine severity, scope, and potential impact. Response and mitigation are immediate actions to reduce impact, like restarting a service or scaling capacity. Resolution confirms full service restoration and documents closure criteria. Finally, post-mortem and learning capture root cause analysis and action items to prevent recurrence. A common misconception is to treat post-mortems as blame sessions; instead, they are fact-based learning exercises with clear action items. For example, if a web tier experiences sustained high C P U, detection might be a CloudWatch alarm. During triage you would check instance metrics and recent deployments. The response could include restarting the process or scaling out the Auto Scaling Group. After service is restored, the post-mortem describes the root cause and updates the runbook. Emphasize measurable closure criteria so everyone agrees when an incident is truly resolved. What measurable signal will you use to close the next incident?

Severity levels are the shorthand your team uses to decide response intensity. The chapter suggests four levels: Severity 1 critical, Severity 2 high, Severity 3 medium, and Severity 4 low. A Severity 1 might be a major service outage with widespread customer impact or data loss, requiring an immediate all-hands response. Severity 2 indicates major functionality is impaired but without data loss, needing urgent attention. Severity 3 covers limited impact with workarounds available and can be scheduled, while Severity 4 is cosmetic or non-urgent. To apply these consistently, use an impact assessment that considers affected user count, financial loss, data integrity, and compliance implications. Misconceptions occur when teams base severity only on loudness — a single high-value customer outage deserves higher severity even if user count is small. Use examples: a degraded payment A P I affecting checkout for 10% of users is higher impact than a cosmetic UI glitch for 90% of users. Document clear thresholds in your incident policy — for instance, number of affected users or error rate percentage — and practice assigning severities during drills. This makes escalation and resource allocation predictable and reduces debate during real incidents.

Runbooks (or playbooks) turn incident knowledge into action. A good runbook includes the incident title and type, clear trigger conditions, a pre-assigned severity, initial triage steps, mitigation steps, troubleshooting, communication and escalation plans, resolution criteria, and post-mortem requirements. This structure ensures responders can act quickly and consistently. The trigger must be specific—naming the alarm and threshold prevents confusion. Initial triage is short and focused: validate the alarm, confirm affected resources, and collect metrics. Mitigation steps are ordered, with safe actions first. Troubleshooting includes deeper diagnostics and commands, while the communication plan lists who to notify and the frequency of updates. Escalation identifies who to call if the primary responder fails to resolve the issue. Keep runbooks living: update them after every incident and after drills. A common misconception is to overload runbooks with too many possible branches; instead, aim for a short, reliable path to reduce cognitive load during stress and reference deeper diagnostics as appendices. Practice the runbook in drills so responders can follow it reflexively. Runbooks: Structure and Best Practices means use concise, ordered steps with clear triggers, mitigation, comms, escalation, and resolution criteria. keep runbooks small and test them.. In practical terms, what each playbook should include and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a simplified runbook for "High C P U on Web Server." The trigger is a CloudWatch alarm named WebTier-HighCPU entering the ALARM state. The initial triage step is to verify the alarm by fetching CPUUtilization for the instance ID and confirming sustained high values. Then check top processes by SSHing into the instance and running top or a process list to identify C P U consumers. Review recent deployments in the CI/CD pipeline to see if a new release correlates with the spike. For mitigation, if the C P U is caused by an application process, restart that service. If it's infrastructure load, scale out the Auto Scaling Group or replace the instance. Communicate status to the incident channel after each major action. Confirm resolution when C P U returns to normal and user errors stop. A misconception is to restart immediately without collecting evidence; instead, gather quick diagnostics first so the post-mortem has context. Practice this runbook, and if you automate any steps, ensure they are reversible and tested in non-production. Below you will see the commands typically used for diagnosis and the mitigation actions as a readable code panel.

Automation can accelerate recovery, but it must be designed and tested carefully. AWS Systems Manager Automation provides runbooks-as-code that perform operations such as restarting instances or scaling groups. Amazon EventBridge acts as the event router: CloudWatch alarms emit a change-of-state event, EventBridge matches it with a rule, and the rule can target an SSM Automation document for execution. A common pattern is to match CloudWatch Alarm State Change events where the alarm name equals your high C P U alarm, then configure the rule to start AWS-RestartEC2Instance or a custom document that scales an Auto Scaling Group. Important safety practices include limiting automation to narrowly scoped actions, using an execution role with least privilege, testing automation in a non-production environment, and designing idempotent steps. A key misconception is to automate wide-ranging destructive actions without reversibility; instead, automate small, reversible remediations first and require manual approval for high-risk changes. Logging automation executions and requiring an approval step for certain conditions preserves control while still enabling fast automated recovery where appropriate. With automation, the biggest risks come from overly broad permissions, untested scripts, or automations that make irreversible changes. A safety example: an Automation document that terminates instances without verifying Auto Scaling Group health can reduce capacity further. To avoid these issues, enforce least-privilege IAM roles for Automation, test documents in non-production, prefer reversible or non-destructive remedial steps, log every execution, and include an approval step for high-risk actions. Practicing runbooks in drills reveals gaps and trains responders. A useful contrast: manual mitigation is slower but safer for complex, novel incidents; automation is faster for well-understood, repeatable problems. Use both thoughtfully — automate the repeatable, keep human oversight for ambiguous situations, and keep your playbooks updated from every post-mortem. We covered the incident lifecycle, severity levels, how to write and maintain runbooks, and how to automate safe remediation using EventBridge and Systems Manager Automation. Remember these three compact ideas: first, adopt the lifecycle Detect → Triage → Respond → Resolve → Learn so incidents become teachable events. Second, define severity by measurable impact—affected users, financial loss, and data risk—and codify thresholds to avoid debate. Third, write concise runbooks with clear triggers, mitigation steps, communication templates, and escalation paths; automate only well-understood, reversible steps with least-privilege execution roles and thorough non-production testing. Common pitfalls include outdated playbooks, broad IAM permissions for automation, and skipping drills. Use post-mortems to close the loop and update your runbooks and automations. Practicing these patterns transforms incident response from ad-hoc firefighting into a repeatable capability that reduces downtime and improves team confidence.

Keep these three reminders close as you apply the chapter. First, make your incident lifecycle explicit and enforce measurable closure criteria so incidents become teachable. Second, define severity using impact metrics and codify thresholds—this avoids lengthy debates when time is scarce. Third, automate only the repeatable and reversible steps: use EventBridge to route alarms to Systems Manager Automation documents that have been tested in non-production and run with least-privilege roles. Together, these rules preserve safety while shortening time-to-recovery.
